stem: A person walks from point P to point Q along a straight road in 10 minutes, then turns back and returns to point R which is midway between P and Q after further 4 minutes. If PQ is 1 km, find the average speed and velocity of the person in going from P to R.
solution:
The path length travelled by the person is 1.5 km while the displacement is the distance between R and P which is 0.5 km. The time taken for the motion is 14 min.

The average speed \(= 1.5 / 14 = 0.107\) km/min \(= 6.42\) km/hr.

The magnitude of the average velocity \(= 0.5/14 = 0.0357\) km/min \(= 2.142\) km/hr.

stem: A stone is thrown vertically upwards from the ground with a velocity 15 m/s. At the same instant a ball is dropped from a point directly above the stone from a height of 30 m. At what height from the ground will the stone and the ball meet and after how much time? (Use \(g = 10\) m/s\(^2\) for ease of calculation).
solution:
Let us assume that the stone and the ball meet after time \(t_0\). The distances (not displacements) travelled by the stone and the ball in that time can be obtained from Eq. (3.8) as

\(s_{\text{stone}} = 15\, t_0 - \dfrac{1}{2}\, g\, t_0^{\,2}\)

\(s_{\text{ball}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\, g\, t_0^{\,2}\)

When they meet, \(s_{\text{stone}} + s_{\text{ball}} = 30\)

\(15\, t_0 - \dfrac{1}{2}\, g\, t_0^{\,2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\, g\, t_0^{\,2} = 30\)

\(t_0 = 30/15 = 2\) s

\(\therefore s_{\text{stone}} = 15\,(2) - \dfrac{1}{2}\,(10)\,(2)^2 = 30 - 20 = 10\) m

Thus the stone and the ball meet at a height of 10 m.
_note: Internal-consistency observation, REPORTED NOT REPAIRED. The printed solution says the quantities are 'The distances (not displacements) travelled', but the expression it then uses, \(s_{\text{stone}} = 15 t_0 - \tfrac{1}{2} g t_0^2\), is the DISPLACEMENT (net rise), not the path length. With \(u = 15\) m/s and \(g = 10\) m/s\(^2\) the stone reaches its highest point at \(t = 1.5\) s (11.25 m) and is already falling at \(t_0 = 2\) s, so its actual distance travelled is \(11.25 + 1.25 = 12.5\) m, not 10 m. The arithmetic and the final answer (they meet at a height of 10 m after 2 s) are correct; only the parenthetical '(not displacements)' contradicts the formula used.

stem: An aeroplane A, is travelling in a straight line with a velocity of 300 km/hr with respect to Earth. Another aeroplane B, is travelling in the opposite direction with a velocity of 350 km/hr with respect to Earth. What is the relative velocity of A with respect to B? What should be the velocity of a third aeroplane C moving parallel to A, relative to the Earth if it has a relative velocity of 100 km/hr with respect to A?
solution:
Let \(v_A\), \(v_B\) and \(v_C\) be the velocities of the three planes relative to the Earth. Relative velocity of A with respect to B \(= v_{AB} = v_A - v_B = 300 - (-350) = 650\) km/hr

Relative velocity of C with respect to A \(= v_{CA} = v_C - v_A = 100\) km/hr.

Thus, \(v_C = v_{CA} + v_A = 400\) km/hr

stem: The position vectors of three particles are given by \(\vec{x}_{1} = (5\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})\) m, \(\vec{x}_{2} = (5t\,\hat{i} + 5t\,\hat{j})\) m and \(\vec{x}_{3} = (5t\,\hat{i} + 10t^{2}\,\hat{j})\) m as a function of time \(t\). Determine the velocity and acceleration for each, in SI units.
solution:
\(\vec{v}_{1} = d\vec{x}_{1}/dt = 0\) as \(\vec{x}_{1}\) does not depend on time t.
Thus, the particle is at rest.
\(\vec{v}_{2} = d\vec{x}_{2}/dt = 5\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}\) m/s. \(\vec{v}_{2}\) does not change with time. \(\therefore \vec{a}_{2} = 0\)
\(v_{2} = \sqrt{5^{2} + 5^{2}} = 5\sqrt{2}\) m/s, \(\tan\theta = 5/5 = 1\) or \(\theta = 45^\circ\). Thus, the direction of \(v_{2}\) makes an angle of \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal.
\(\vec{v}_{3} = d\vec{x}_{3}/dt = 5\hat{i} + 20t\,\hat{j}\).
\(\therefore v_{3} = \sqrt{5^{2} + (20t)^{2}}\) m/s. Its direction is along \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{20t}{5}\right)\) with the horizontal.
\(\vec{a}_{3} = \dfrac{d\vec{v}_{3}}{dt} = 20\hat{j}\) m/s\(^{2}\)
Thus, the particle 3 is getting accelerated along the \(y\)-axis at 20 m/s\(^{2}\).
_note: The book denotes the POSITION vectors by \(\vec{x}_{1}, \vec{x}_{2}, \vec{x}_{3}\) (not the usual \(\vec{r}\)); transcribed as printed - do not "correct" it. Printed derivation checked for internal consistency and NO discrepancy found: \(d(5t\hat{i}+10t^{2}\hat{j})/dt = 5\hat{i}+20t\hat{j}\), \(\sqrt{5^{2}+5^{2}} = 5\sqrt{2}\), \(\tan^{-1}1 = 45^\circ\), and \(d(5\hat{i}+20t\hat{j})/dt = 20\hat{j}\) all hold. The book states particle 1 is at rest but never writes \(\vec{a}_{1} = 0\) explicitly. Stem heading is on p-07; the whole Solution is on p-08 (band boundary crossed as briefed).

stem: An aeroplane is travelling northward with a speed of 300 km/hr with respect to the Earth, when the wind is blowing from east to west at a speed of 100 km/hr. What is the velocity of the aeroplane with respect to the wind?
solution:
Let the velocity of the aeroplane with respect to Earth be \(\vec{v}_{AE}\), velocity of wind with respect to Earth be \(\vec{v}_{WE}\). The velocity of aeroplane with respect to wind, \(\vec{v}_{AW}\) can be determined by the following expression:
\(\vec{v}_{AW} = \vec{v}_{AE} + \vec{v}_{EW} = \vec{v}_{AE} - \vec{v}_{WE} = 100\hat{i} + 300\hat{j}\), considering north along \(+y\) axis.
Magnitude of \(\vec{v}_{AW} = \sqrt{\left(10000 + 90000\right)} = 100\sqrt{10}\) km/hr, and its direction, \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{300}{100}\right) = 71.6^\circ\) is towards north of east.
_note: Printed derivation checked for internal consistency and NO discrepancy found: with \(\vec{v}_{AE} = 300\hat{j}\) and a wind blowing east-to-west \(\vec{v}_{WE} = -100\hat{i}\), so \(\vec{v}_{AE} - \vec{v}_{WE} = 100\hat{i} + 300\hat{j}\); \(\sqrt{10000+90000} = \sqrt{100000} = 100\sqrt{10}\); \(\tan^{-1}3 = 71.57^\circ\). Stem is in the LEFT column of p-09, its Solution at the TOP of the RIGHT column of the same page - reading across the page would separate them.

stem: A stone is thrown with an initial velocity components of 20 m/s along the vertical, and 15 m/s along the horizontal direction. Determine the position and velocity of the stone after 3 s. Determine the maximum height that it will reach and the total distance travelled along the horizontal on reaching the ground. (Assume \(g = 10\) m/s\(^2\))
solution:
The initial velocity of the stone in x-direction \(= u \cos\theta = 15\) m/s and in y-direction \(= u \sin\theta = 20\) m/s.

After 3 s, \(v_x = u \cos\theta = 15\) m/s and \(v_y = u \sin\theta - gt = 20 - 10(3) = -10\) m/s \(= 10\) m/s downwards.

\(\therefore v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{15^2 + 10^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{225 + 100} = \sqrt{325}\)

\(= 18.03\) m/s

\(\tan\alpha = v_y / v_x = 10/15 = 2/3\)

\(\therefore \alpha = \tan^{-1}(2/3) = 33^\circ\ 41'\) with the horizontal.

\(s_x = (u \cos\theta)\, t = 15 \times 3 = 45\) m,

\(s_y = (u \sin\theta)\, t - \frac{1}{2} gt^2 = 20 \times 3 - 5(3)^2 = 15\) m.

Thus the stone will be at a distance 45 m along horizontal and 15 m along vertical direction from the initial position after time 3 s. The velocity is 18.03 m/s making an angle \(33^\circ\ 41'\) with the horizontal.

The maximum vertical distance travelled is given by \(H = (u \sin\theta)^2/(2g) = 20^2/(2 \times 10) = 20\) m

Maximum horizontal distance travelled

\(R = 2.u_x.u_y/g = 2(15)(20)/10 = 60\) m
_note: Printed derivation checked for internal consistency and it is CLEAN — every printed value reproduces exactly: sqrt(325) = 18.0278 -> 18.03, tan^-1(2/3) = 33.690 deg = 33 deg 41.4 min -> 33 deg 41', s_x = 45, s_y = 60 - 45 = 15, H = 400/20 = 20, R = 600/10 = 60. Two NOTATIONAL observations only (not arithmetic errors, transcribed verbatim, not repaired): (1) the book writes 'v_y = ... = -10 m/s = 10 m/s downwards', equating a signed component to a magnitude-plus-direction; (2) the stem's grammar slip 'an initial velocity components' is the book's own. Layout note: the last line of this solution ('Maximum horizontal distance travelled / R = ...= 60 m') is printed at the TOP OF THE RIGHT COLUMN of p-11, not at the foot of the left column; a left-column-only read would truncate the solution before R.

stem: An object of mass 50 g moves uniformly along a circular orbit with an angular speed of 5 rad/s. If the linear speed of the particle is 25 m/s, what is the radius of the circle? Calculate the centripetal force acting on the particle.
solution:
The linear speed and angular speed are related by \(v = \omega r\)

\(\therefore r = v/\omega = 25/5\) m \(= 5\) m.

Centripetal force acting on the object \(= \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{0.05 \times 25^2}{5} = 6.25\) N.

stem: An object is travelling in a horizontal circle with uniform speed. At \(t = 0\), the velocity is given by \(\vec{u} = 20\hat{i} + 35\hat{j}\) km/s. After one minute the velocity becomes \(\vec{v} = -20\hat{i} - 35\hat{j}\). What is the magnitude of the acceleration?
solution:
Magnitude of initial and final velocities =

\(= u = \sqrt{(20)^2 + (35)^2}\) m/s

\(= \sqrt{1625}\) m/s

\(= 40.3\) m/s

As the velocity reverses in 1 min, the time period of revolution is 2 min.

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{u}\), giving \(r = \dfrac{uT}{2\pi}\)

\(a = \dfrac{u^2}{r} = \dfrac{u^2\,2\pi}{uT} = \dfrac{2\pi u}{T} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14 \times 40.3}{2 \times 60}\)

\(= 2.11\) m s\(^{-2}\)
_note: UNIT INCONSISTENCY IN THE PRINTED QUESTION vs ITS OWN SOLUTION (reported, not repaired). The stem prints the initial velocity as \(\vec{u} = 20\hat{i} + 35\hat{j}\) km/s, but the printed solution computes the magnitude as \(\sqrt{(20)^2+(35)^2}\) m/s = \(\sqrt{1625}\) m/s = 40.3 m/s and carries m/s through to the final 2.11 m s\(^{-2}\). If the stem's km/s were honoured the answer would be 2110 m s\(^{-2}\) (2.11 km s\(^{-2}\)). Also: the final velocity \(\vec{v} = -20\hat{i} - 35\hat{j}\) is printed with NO unit at all. Separately, the solution's first equation line opens with a stray leading '=' ('= u = \(\sqrt{\ldots}\)') after the words 'Magnitude of initial and final velocities ='. ARITHMETIC ITSELF IS CONSISTENT: \(\sqrt{1625} = 40.31\) (printed 40.3); with T = 2 min = 120 s, \(2\pi u/T = 2\times3.14\times40.3/120 = 2.109\) (printed 2.11), and the book's own struck-through cancellation of the two 2's gives the same value.
